headline: Two Dan Sullivans. Now the US is suing Alaska.
summary: Alaska's Senate race has Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, Democrat Mary Peltola, and a retired teacher also named Dan Sullivan. On Thursday the Justice Department sued to stop Alaska certifying the result if the senator loses by less than the other Sullivan's votes. Trump: "I'm the one that said do it." The vote is November 3.

cover_question.q: Why are there two Dan Sullivans?

cover_answer: Two men share a name. Both want the same job.
table_question: If two players had the same name, how would you keep the score fair?

5-7.script: In Alaska, two men named Dan Sullivan both want the same job, senator, and both names will be on the voting paper. The president's lawyers worry people will tick the wrong Dan by mistake, like two kids in a class with the same name getting each other's homework back. They have asked a judge to step in, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Two Dans, one job, a mix-up. The judge is the grown-up in the room.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, and two children with one name in a class is in front of them most days, so the script makes that the whole story and leaves the courts to the older cards. Expect "which Dan is the real one?" Both are real. One has the job now, and the vote decides who has it next.

8-12.script: Senator Dan Sullivan is in a close race with Democrat Mary Peltola. A third man, also Dan Sullivan, got 4,107 votes in the primary, about 2 percent. So the Justice Department sued: if the senator loses by less than that, hold the result, like a referee holding the whistle for a replay.
8-12.why: 2 percent, a photo finish, a replay review. Then: who gets to call it?
8-12.why_long: At this age a child is working out rules and who applies them, and this story is that: Alaska's courts said the second Sullivan stays, and now Washington asks a different referee for a different call. The 4,107 votes make the chain concrete. Expect "can they just not count it?" A law professor says the law does not let them.

13-17.script: Should Washington get a say in whether a state certifies its own election? The Justice Department sued to stop Alaska certifying a Peltola win if Senator Dan Sullivan loses by less than the votes for the other Dan Sullivan. Second: Trump says he ordered it. Fair ask, or sore loser's?
13-17.why: States run elections, and a president ordered a suit. Hold both.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things: a same-name candidate really could tip a photo finish, and a president who says he ordered the suit has a stake in the result. The script asks them to carry both and say what would make the ask fair. Expect "is this how he'd stop a loss anywhere?" Blanche says not outside extreme cases.

5-7.q: Why are there two Dan Sullivans?
5-7.a: Two different men happen to share a name, and both want the same job. One is the senator; the other is a retired teacher.

8-12.q: Can two people have the same name on a ballot?
8-12.a: Yes. Alaska's top court kept the second Sullivan on, with no party label.
Making the count official. The suit wants it paused in a narrow loss.

13-17.q: Is the second Dan Sullivan a plant?
13-17.a: Republicans say so. He says he ran on his own.
Notre Dame's Derek Muller says the law doesn't allow it.
